contentBlocks.text: You've learned ionic bonding's electron transfer. Today: covalent bonding, where atoms share instead!

Covalent bonding happens when atoms share, rather than transfer, electrons — this typically occurs between two nonmetal atoms that both need more electrons to complete their octet, so neither can simply give one away. In water (H₂O), each hydrogen atom shares one electron with oxygen, and oxygen shares one electron with each hydrogen, so all three atoms effectively get a more complete outer shell through sharing. Explain why sharing, rather than transferring, makes more sense when two atoms both need additional electrons rather than one having extra to give away.
You just learned how covalent bonding works! Tomorrow we'll compare ionic and covalent bonds directly.

objectives: Describe covalent bonding as electron sharing between atoms
Explain why sharing makes sense when both atoms need additional electrons
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review this week's octet-rule and ionic-bonding work.
2. Introduce covalent bonding using the water (H₂O) example.
3. Have the child explain why sharing makes sense in this case.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's ionic-vs-covalent comparison.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use a simple real-world analogy — if two people both need one more dollar to afford something, pooling their money (sharing) makes more sense than one just giving theirs away
Ready for more: ask the child to predict whether two identical nonmetal atoms (like two oxygen atoms) could form a covalent bond with each other
This is a genuinely important contrast with yesterday's ionic bonding — worth emphasizing the mechanism difference, not just the vocabulary
teacherGuide.answerKey: When both atoms need additional electrons to complete their octet, transferring an electron away wouldn't help the giving atom get closer to a full shell — sharing lets both atoms count the shared electrons toward their own octet at the same time, benefiting both without either one having to give anything away permanently.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses NGSS Grade 9-10 standard HS-PS1-3, contrasting covalent bonding's sharing mechanism with yesterday's ionic bonding.
